# Agent-based models

An agent-based model (ABM) represents a population as interacting individuals.
The SIR labels remain familiar, but the model now exposes who contacts whom,
when an agent changes status, and how an update schedule can affect results.
This chapter uses a deliberately small, well-mixed ABM so that the connection
to the population equations stays visible.

## Learning goals

You will:

- classify an individual-level SIR model and distinguish it from a count model;
- implement a synchronous contact-and-recovery rule with Agents.jl 7;
- collect model-level data with the current `StandardABM` and `run!` APIs; and
- compare an ensemble of individual simulations with the deterministic SIR
  ODE while identifying effects that aggregation hides.

## Model assumptions and classification

The population has $N=1000$ named individuals. Initially 10 are infectious,
990 are susceptible, and none are recovered. At every $\Delta t=0.1$ time
unit, a susceptible makes $K\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(c\Delta t)$ random
contacts. A contact chooses a uniformly random individual and transmits with
probability $\beta$ if that individual is infectious. An infectious agent
recovers with probability $1-\exp(-\gamma\Delta t)$. Recovered agents are
immune. We use $c=10$, $\beta=0.05$, and $\gamma=0.25$.

This is a **stochastic, discrete-time, discrete-state, individual-level**
model. Time is discrete because `StandardABM` advances in integer steps;
state is discrete because each `Person.status` is one of `:S`, `:I`, or `:R`.
The population is well mixed because the model has no spatial structure:
`StandardABM(Person)` uses the `nothing` space. This is an ABM even though
its aggregated contact rule is designed to approximate mass action.

## Equations

Let $Z_i(t)\in\{S,I,R\}$ be individual $i$'s status and
$I_t=\sum_i\mathbf{1}(Z_i(t)=I)$. For a susceptible, the probability of no
successful transmission in one step, conditional on $K_i=k$, is

$$
 \left(1-\beta\frac{I_t}{N}\right)^k.
$$

Averaging over $K_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(c\Delta t)$ gives

$$
 \Pr(Z_i(t+\Delta t)=I\mid Z_i(t)=S)
 =1-\exp\!\left[-c\Delta t\,\beta\frac{I_t}{N}\right].
$$ {#eq-abm-infection}

The recovery probability is
$$
\Pr(Z_i(t+\Delta t)=R\mid Z_i(t)=I)=1-\exp(-\gamma\Delta t).
$$

For small $\Delta t$, Equation @eq-abm-infection is approximately
$\beta c(I_t/N)\Delta t$, matching the SIR force of infection. The
individual model contains more information than the population equations:
the identity of every contact and every infection is retained. The ODE only
tracks the totals and uses the deterministic flow
$$
\dot S=-\beta cSI/N,\qquad
\dot I=\beta cSI/N-\gamma I,\qquad
\dot R=\gamma I.
$$

## Julia implementation

Agents.jl 7 requires the `@agent` macro for supported agent types. In the
installed 7.0.3 API, `NoSpaceAgent` contributes the mandatory `id` field;
`StandardABM(Person; agent_step!, model_step!, properties, rng)` constructs a
discrete-time model. We use a two-phase update: `agent_step!` reads the old
statuses and writes `next_status`, then `model_step!` commits all changes.
Without this separation, activation order could let a newly infected agent
transmit in the same step.

```{julia}
#| label: code-ch06-setup
using Agents
using CairoMakie
using Distributions
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using StableRNGs
using Statistics

const N = 1000
const I₀ = 10
const β = 0.05
const c = 10.0
const γ = 0.25
const Δt = 0.1
const nsteps = 300
const times = collect(0.0:Δt:(nsteps * Δt))

@agent struct Person(NoSpaceAgent)
    status::Symbol
    next_status::Symbol
end
```

The contact loop uses the model's random-number generator through
`abmrng(model)`. `random_agent(model)` is the current Agents.jl helper for
uniformly selecting an agent from a no-space model.

```{julia}
#| label: code-ch06-rules
function agent_step!(person, model)
    person.next_status = person.status
    if person.status == :S
        for _ in 1:rand(abmrng(model), Poisson(model.c * model.Δt))
            contact = random_agent(model)
            if contact.status == :I && rand(abmrng(model)) < model.β
                person.next_status = :I
                break
            end
        end
    elseif person.status == :I
        if rand(abmrng(model)) < 1 - exp(-model.γ * model.Δt)
            person.next_status = :R
        end
    end
    return nothing
end

function model_step!(model)
    for person in allagents(model)
        person.status = person.next_status
    end
    return nothing
end

susceptible_count(model) = count(person.status == :S for person in allagents(model))
infected_count(model) = count(person.status == :I for person in allagents(model))
recovered_count(model) = count(person.status == :R for person in allagents(model))
```

The model properties are a named tuple, so `model.β`, `model.c`, and
`model.Δt` are ordinary Julia field accesses. The `mdata` functions below are
called by `run!` at the initial state and after each step.

```{julia}
#| label: code-ch06-constructor
function initialize_model(seed)
    model = StandardABM(
        Person;
        agent_step!,
        model_step!,
        properties = (β = β, c = c, γ = γ, Δt = Δt),
        rng = StableRNG(seed),
    )
    for id in 1:N
        status = id <= I₀ ? :I : :S
        add_agent!(Person(; id, status, next_status = status), model)
    end
    return model
end

model = initialize_model(20250711)
agent_data, model_data = run!(
    model,
    nsteps;
    mdata = [susceptible_count, infected_count, recovered_count],
    showprogress = false,
)
```

`run!` returns two data frames: one for agent observations and one for model
observations. We requested only model-level totals, which keeps the example
small while retaining the full individual state inside the model. The first
row is the initial condition because `init=true` is the default.

```{julia}
#| label: code-ch06-ode
abm_states = Matrix(model_data[:, [
    :susceptible_count, :infected_count, :recovered_count,
]])'
abm_times = Float64.(model_data.time) .* Δt

function sir_drift!(du, u, p, t)
    β, c, γ, N = p
    infection = β * c * u[1] * u[2] / N
    du[1] = -infection
    du[2] = infection - γ * u[2]
    du[3] = γ * u[2]
    return nothing
end

ode_problem = ODEProblem(
    sir_drift!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], (0.0, nsteps * Δt), (β, c, γ, N),
)
ode_solution = solve(ode_problem, Tsit5(); saveat = abm_times)
ode_states = Array(ode_solution)
```

The model time reported by a discrete `StandardABM` is the step number, so
the explicit multiplication by $\Delta t$ maps it to the physical time used
by the ODE.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ch06-abm
#| fig-cap: "One individual-based SIR realization and the corresponding ODE trajectory."
fig = Figure(size = (760, 430))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "time", ylabel = "people",
    title = "Well-mixed individual-based SIR")
for (j, (name, color)) in enumerate(zip(["S", "I", "R"],
                                         [:steelblue, :firebrick, :seagreen]))
    stairs!(ax, abm_times, abm_states[j, :]; color, linewidth = 2,
        label = "$name (ABM)")
    lines!(ax, abm_times, ode_states[j, :]; color, linestyle = :dash,
        linewidth = 1.5, label = "$name (ODE)")
end
axislegend(ax, position = :rt, nbanks = 2)
fig
```

## Validation

The ABM has an exact bookkeeping invariant: every person has exactly one
status. Consequently $S+I+R=N$ at every recorded step.

```{julia}
#| label: code-ch06-validation
population_error = maximum(abs.(vec(sum(abm_states; dims = 1)) .- N))
@assert population_error == 0
@assert minimum(abm_states) >= 0
(; population_error, final_counts = abm_states[:, end])
```

One realization can differ substantially from the ODE. To compare levels
rather than a single random path, run a small deterministic ensemble. The
model constructor gives each replicate its own seeded random stream.

```{julia}
#| label: code-ch06-ensemble
function simulate_abm(seed)
    model = initialize_model(seed)
    _, data = run!(
        model,
        nsteps;
        mdata = [susceptible_count, infected_count, recovered_count],
        showprogress = false,
    )
    return Matrix(data[:, [
        :susceptible_count, :infected_count, :recovered_count,
    ]])'
end

abm_ensemble = cat((simulate_abm(4000 + k) for k in 1:16)...; dims = 3)
abm_mean = dropdims(mean(abm_ensemble; dims = 3), dims = 3)
infectious_rmse = sqrt(mean((abm_mean[2, :] .- ode_states[2, :]).^2))
@assert maximum(abs.(sum(abm_ensemble; dims = 1) .- N)) == 0
infectious_rmse
```

The comparison is intentionally modest: 16 paths are enough to reveal the
relationship and keep a teaching render quick, but not enough for a narrow
confidence interval.

## Interpretation and limitations

The ABM can be extended by replacing the no-space model with a grid, network,
or continuous space, or by adding age, behavior, vaccination, or household
fields to `Person`. Those extensions change who can contact whom and can
create clustering, superspreading, and spatial waves that a mass-action ODE
cannot represent. The price is computational and inferential: agent rules
need careful calibration, contact mechanisms can be difficult to observe, and
random seeds do not remove structural uncertainty.

Our synchronous two-phase update avoids an order artifact, but the contact
rule still samples with replacement and allows self-contact. For $N=1000$
this is a small approximation; a network model would make contact constraints
explicit. The model is also discrete in time, so $\Delta t$ should be
reduced and results checked for timestep sensitivity. Agents.jl's
[agent definition documentation](https://juliadynamics.github.io/Agents.jl/v7.0.3/agents/)
and [data collection documentation](https://juliadynamics.github.io/Agents.jl/v7.0.3/data/)
describe the v7 `@agent`, `StandardABM`, and `run!` APIs. The framework and
its modeling rationale are described by Datseris, Vahdati, and DuBois
[@datseris2022].

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 {#ch06-ex1}

Change `initialize_model` to create a two-dimensional `GridSpace`, add a
position field using the v7 `@agent` syntax, and let each susceptible contact
only an agent in a Moore neighborhood. Keep the same infection and recovery
parameters, verify $S+I+R=N$, and explain which assumption in Equation
@eq-abm-infection is no longer valid.

### Exercise 2 {#ch06-ex2}

Run the ABM with $\Delta t=0.2$, $0.1$, and $0.05$, keeping physical
time fixed. For each value, use at least 16 seeded replicates and calculate
the ensemble mean and standard deviation of the peak infectious count.
Compare those summaries with the ODE peak and discuss whether changing the
update interval changes numerical error, biological assumptions, or both.
